query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an in‐situ engineered dual‐phase microstructure—with a finely dispersed ductile phase network at grain boundaries—will arrest crack propagation and improve mechanical integrity of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38, without degrading its intrinsic large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting excellent caloric response under applied magnetic or pressure fields but with poor mechanical integrity (brittleness and crack susceptibility).
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy’s solidification and/or thermomechanical processing to promote the in-situ precipitation of a ductile second phase that forms a continuous, finely dispersed network along the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Operation under applied magnetic and pressure fields near the alloy’s caloric transition temperature, and mechanical testing under compressive regimes similar to prior epoxy- and In-based composite tests (targeting compressive strengths above 150 MPa).
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure where a ductile second phase, finely distributed along grain boundaries, coexists with the primary caloric phase.
generation.mechanism: The ductile network at the boundaries will effectively absorb and blunt stress concentrations, arresting crack propagation during mechanical loading without interfering with the phase transition responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit increased compressive strength (ideally approaching or surpassing the 152–218 MPa range observed in epoxy-containing systems) and improved fracture resistance while maintaining a caloric response comparable in magnitude to the original material.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or conventionally processed (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with high caloric performance but poor mechanical robustness.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected under operational conditions that include applied magnetic/pressure fields near the caloric transition temperature and typical mechanical loadings; extreme conditions beyond the calibrated processing window may lead to different phase formations.
generation.uncertainty: The interplay between the newly introduced ductile phase and the caloric transformation remains partially uncertain, including potential minor alterations in transition temperatures or caloric effect magnitude. Precise quantitative improvements in compressive strength and any slight compromise, if present, in caloric performance are not fully predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one processed via conventional methods and another using the modified solidification/thermomechanical route optimized to induce an in-situ ductile grain-boundary phase. Subject both sets to identical tests under applied magnetic/pressure fields and standard compressive loading. Compare their compressive strengths, fracture behaviors, and caloric response magnitudes.
measurements: Compressive strength (in MPa) via quasi-static compression tests
Crack initiation and propagation behavior, monitored using high-resolution in-situ imaging during loading
Caloric effect magnitude (e.g., temperature change or entropy change) under applied fields
Transition temperature of the caloric effect
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength and crack resistance (e.g., achieving values comparable to or above ~152 MPa) or if the caloric response is reduced by more than a minor, acceptable margin relative to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have gained widespread concern in response to the increased requirements for future high-temperature structural superalloys. By combining phase-diagram calculations with microhardness, compression behavior measurements at room temperature, and elevated temperature conditions, the very important role of the Cr element on the microstructure and properties is deeply revealed, which provides candidates materials for future high-temperature alloy applications. The increment of Cr favors the regulation of the two-phase fraction and distribution. The thermodynamic calculations illustrate that the density and melting point of the HEAs showed an increasing trend with the increase of the Cr content. The typical worm-like microstructure of the Cr0.6 alloy with a dual BCC structure was detected. Meanwhile, on the one hand, the increment of the Cr elements results in a considerable optimization of the mechanical properties of the alloy in terms of strength and ductility at room temperature. frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy, which exhibits a large caloric response under applied magnetic/pressure fields but suffers from inherent brittleness and cracking.
frame.goal: To achieve a material that combines high caloric performance with robust mechanical integrity (improved compressive strength and resistance to cracking) while remaining rare-earth-free.
frame.limitation: The alloy’s poor structural integrity and tendency to crack limit its practical application, despite its desirable caloric properties.
root_cause_cues: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: cannot sacrifice the high caloric response
must operate under applied-field and pressure-field conditions similar to previous tests
needs to achieve or exceed the compressive strength improvements seen in epoxy- or In-containing composites
frame.regime: Testing under operational conditions including applied magnetic/pressure fields near the caloric transition temperature and mechanical loading within compressive strength regimes (as referenced by compressive strengths of 152–218 MPa for epoxy-containing systems versus 48 MPa for low-melting In composites).
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites that improved compressive strengths up to 218 MPa but may compromise other properties due to the organic phase.
Low-melting In composites that enhanced thermal conductivity (8× that of epoxy systems) while failing to provide adequate compressive strength (only 48 MPa).

families.principle: Designing the intrinsic microstructure—such as engineered grain size, distribution, and the in-situ formation of ductile second-phase networks—can reconcile high caloric performance with enhanced mechanical toughness.
cues_for: the explicit mention of 'poor integrity' and 'tends to crack'
the unresolved challenge of concurrently achieving robust mechanical properties and high caloric response
cues_against: previous composite attempts relied on extrinsic additives rather than in-situ microstructural control
families.best_lever: Engineer an in-situ microstructure with a dual-phase architecture where a finely dispersed ductile network forms at grain boundaries during solidification, effectively arresting crack propagation without compromising the caloric phase transition.

families.principle: Altering the elemental makeup can stabilize phases and promote intrinsic ductility by forming beneficial solid‐solution or second phases without introducing extrinsic additives.
cues_for: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance

families.best_lever: Introduce a minor, ductility‐promoting alloying element (for example, a low concentration of Cu or Al) that forms a coherent, toughening phase while preserving the caloric response.

families.principle: Adjusting synthesis conditions (e.g., cooling rate, consolidation pressure, and temperature) can refine microstructure and diminish defects, which in turn may improve mechanical integrity.
cues_for: the alloy’s inherent poor structural integrity and tendency to crack
cues_against: the question and prior work focus on modifications beyond synthesis, for instance by adding composites
families.best_lever: Adopt a high-pressure, high-temperature sintering or rapid solidification process to obtain a fine-grained, defect‐minimized microstructure that improves toughness under operational field conditions.

families.principle: Post-synthesis heat or deformation treatments can induce precipitate formation and relieve residual stresses, which may improve ductility or toughness.
cues_for: the need for robust mechanical performance under applied-field and pressure conditions
cues_against: danger of shifting the caloric phase transformation characteristics if the treatment is too aggressive
prior attempts using external additives suggest that simple thermal steps may not suffice
families.best_lever: Implement a carefully optimized annealing/deformation sequence that precipitates a secondary ductile phase without interfering with the caloric transition temperature.

families.principle: Tailoring surfaces or interfacial bonding (for instance, through coatings or intergranular films) can hinder crack initiation and propagation, thereby enhancing toughness.
cues_for: the description of cracking tendencies and poor integrity
cues_against: the need for bulk improvement rather than just surface reinforcement
the intervention must not affect the intrinsic caloric response which is governed by the bulk phase transformation
families.best_lever: Employ a thin, robust intergranular coating or engineered grain-boundary phase to reinforce the interface areas, though its impact may be limited if only surface effects are engaged.
